The EM algorithm¶

Three worked examples of maximum likelihood estimation with a latent (unobserved) variable:

  1. A two-coin example - the smallest possible EM, where the latent variable is which coin was tossed.
  2. Allele frequencies from genotype likelihoods - the same algorithm on sequencing data, where the latent variable is the genotype.
  3. The maximum likelihood of a binomial - a recap of what a likelihood is and where its maximum lies, with an analytical solution. No latent variable and no EM, so read this part first if the word likelihood is new to you.

1. A two-coin example¶

The example and its data are from Do CB & Batzoglou S (2008), What is the expectation maximization algorithm?, Nature Biotechnology 26:897-899.

We observe outcomes from 5 independent sequences of 10 coin tosses each. For each sequence, an unobserved choice is made between two biased coins, A and B, and then that chosen coin is tossed 10 times. We see the tosses but not which coin generated each sequence.

Data (5 sequences):

sequence tosses (number of heads)
HTTTHHTHTH 5
HHHHTHHHHH 9
HTHHHHHTHH 8
HTHTTTHHTT 4
THHHTHHHTH 7

Model¶

  • Latent variable for sequence :
    indicating which coin was used.
  • Parameters:
    • Coin usage frequency: . For now we assume both coins are equally likely, , so . In Bonus 2 we estimate instead of assuming it.
    • Coin frequencies of heads: , .

For sequence , let be the number of heads and the number of tails, obtained by counting the H and T in the string.

The likelihood of one sequence, given the coin that produced it, is:

EM Algorithm¶

Initialize (e.g. ).

E-step (compute expectations)¶

For each sequence , compute the posterior probability that coin A (or B) generated it given theta from the th step in the algorithm. In each step we need to find the posterior probablity of the latent state which is also denoted :

Then .

M-step (maximize expected complete-data log-likelihood)¶

Update parameters using weighted counts (weights = responsibilities):

Iterate E-step and M-step until convergence of the log-likelihood or parameters. here "(n)" refers to the th step in the EM algorithm

Applying to the Given Data¶

  1. Count heads and tails for each sequence. Each sequence has heads and tails.
  2. Run EM using the formulas above:
    • E-step: compute for all 5 sequences.
    • M-step: update .
  3. Repeat until parameter changes are negligible (e.g., ).

Notes¶

  • EM is guaranteed to not decrease the data log-likelihood each iteration.
  • Different initializations can converge to different local optima, so try a few starts to check stability.

The data. None is read from disk — every example simulates or types in its own numbers, so the notebook runs anywhere.

  • What are Z , X and θ ?
  • What is P(X|Z,θ)
  • What is P(Z|X,θ) ?
  • What is P(Z|θ) ?
In [1]:
EMcoinStep<-function(theta,data){
  lik <- cbind(#likelihood of data assuming
    dbinom(data,10,theta[1]), #coin A
    dbinom(data,10,theta[2]) #coin B
  )
  ##probabilty of coin given data
  wA<-lik[,1]*0.5 / (lik[,1]*0.5 + lik[,2]*0.5)
  wB<-lik[,2]*0.5 / (lik[,1]*0.5 + lik[,2]*0.5)
  newTheta <-c(#n+1 - parameter
    sum(data*wA)/sum(data*wA + (10-data)*wA),
    sum(data*wB)/sum(data*wB + (10-data)*wB)
  )
  return(newTheta)
}

data <- c(5,9,8,4,7)   # number of heads in each of the 5 sequences

## theta is c(theta_A, theta_B), the two coins' probabilities of heads.
## Same starting point as the text above: theta_A=0.6, theta_B=0.5
theta <- c(0.6,0.5)
for(i in 1:100)
  print(theta<-EMcoinStep(theta,data))

The same run, as a picture¶

The two panels below are our own version of the walk-through in Figure 1 of the article, drawn from the numbers this notebook just produced.

  • Left, the E-step. For each of the 5 sequences, how probable it is that coin A rather than coin B produced it, at the first iteration. The sequence with 9 heads is probably the biased coin A (), the one with 4 heads probably coin B (). Nothing here is observed - these are the weights the algorithm invents for itself, and they are what stands in for the coin labels we do not have.
  • Right, the M-step. Each iteration re-estimates the two coins using those weights, and the estimates settle down after about 6 iterations.

Compare the five left-hand numbers and the two final estimates with Figure 1 of the article.

In [2]:
## our own version of the walk-through in Figure 1 of Do & Batzoglou (2008),
## drawn from the run above

colA <- "#2a78d6"; colB <- "#eb6834"      # colourblind-safe pair
ink  <- "#52514e"; grid_col <- "#e4e4e1"

start <- c(0.6,0.5)                        # theta_A, theta_B before the first iteration

## the E-step weights at the first iteration: q(Z_i = A) for each sequence
likA <- dbinom(data,10,start[1])
likB <- dbinom(data,10,start[2])
wA   <- likA*0.5/(likA*0.5 + likB*0.5)

## run the EM again, this time keeping every iteration
maxIter <- 10
traj <- matrix(NA,maxIter+1,2)
theta <- start
traj[1,] <- theta
for(i in 1:maxIter){
  theta <- EMcoinStep(theta,data)
  traj[i+1,] <- theta
}

par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4.5,4.6,3.8,1.5), mgp=c(2.7,0.7,0), tcl=-0.25,
    col.axis=ink, col.lab=ink, fg=ink, las=1)

## ---- left panel: the E step
bp <- barplot(rbind(wA,1-wA), col=c(colA,colB), border="white", space=0.35,
   names.arg=paste0("X", 1:5, "\n", data, " heads"), ylim=c(0,1.2), yaxt="n",
   ylab="posterior of the coin,  q(Z)",
   main="E-step: which coin made each sequence?", cex.names=0.85, font.main=1)
axis(2, at=seq(0,1,0.2))
text(bp, wA/2,        sprintf("%.2f",wA),   col="white", cex=0.8)
text(bp, wA+(1-wA)/2, sprintf("%.2f",1-wA), col="white", cex=0.8)
legend("top", c("coin A","coin B"), fill=c(colA,colB), border="white",
       horiz=TRUE, bty="n", text.col=ink, cex=0.85)

## ---- right panel: the M step
plot(NA, xlim=c(0,maxIter), ylim=c(0.45,0.85), xlab="EM iteration",
     ylab="probability of heads", main="M-step: the estimates converging",
     font.main=1, xaxs="i")
abline(h=seq(0.5,0.85,0.05), col=grid_col)
abline(h=traj[maxIter+1,], col=c(colA,colB), lty=3)
matlines(0:maxIter, traj, type="b", pch=16, lty=1, lwd=2, cex=0.9, col=c(colA,colB))
text(maxIter, traj[maxIter+1,1], sprintf("%.3f",traj[maxIter+1,1]), adj=c(1,-0.9), col=ink, cex=0.8)
text(maxIter, traj[maxIter+1,2], sprintf("%.3f",traj[maxIter+1,2]), adj=c(1,1.7),  col=ink, cex=0.8)
legend("right", legend=c(expression(theta[A]), expression(theta[B])),
       col=c(colA,colB), lwd=2, pch=16, bty="n", text.col=ink, cex=0.9)

par(mfrow=c(1,1))

Bonus 2 - What if we don't know the coin probability¶

instead of assuming the coin probability is 0.5 we can estimate it from the data

In [3]:
EMcoinStep2<-function(theta,data){
  pA <- theta[3]
  pB <- 1-pA
  lik <- cbind(#likelihood of data assuming
    dbinom(data,10,theta[1]), #coin A
    dbinom(data,10,theta[2]) #coin B
  )
  ##probabilty of coin given data
  wA<-lik[,1]*pA / (lik[,1]*pA + lik[,2]*pB)
  wB<-lik[,2]*pB / (lik[,1]*pA + lik[,2]*pB)
  newTheta <-c(#n+1 - parameter
    sum(data*wA)/sum(data*wA + (10-data)*wA),
    sum(data*wB)/sum(data*wB + (10-data)*wB),
    sum(wA)/length(data)
  )
  return(newTheta)
}

data <- c(5,9,8,4,7)
## theta is c(theta_A, theta_B, pi) where pi = p(coin = A) is now estimated too
theta <- c(0.6,0.5,0.9)
for(i in 1:100)
  print(theta<-EMcoinStep2(theta,data))

2. Estimating allele frequencies from genotype likelihoods¶

We will try to estimate allele frequencies from the reads of 6 individuals, as in the "Simple allele frequency estimator" slide. The number of reads supporting allele C and allele T is shown in the table

individuals 1 2 3 4 5 6
C reads 7 25 5 4 0 0
T reads 0 1 3 4 2 4

To simplify we will assume that the sequencing error rate is for all reads (Not recommended for real data) and we will use the GATK model so that . When the error rates are the same for each reads and we only observe two kinds of read then the GATK model simplifies to

Which allele frequency are we estimating? This site has two alleles, C and T, so there is only one free frequency parameter. Throughout this exercise we estimate the frequency of the T allele and call it . The frequency of the C allele is then . Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium the genotype probabilities are therefore

i.e. the genotype counts the number of T alleles (0, 1 or 2). Note that estimating is equivalent to estimating - you just have to keep track of which allele you are counting.

You can read and run the calculations in R below

In [5]:
e <-0.01
Creads <- c(7,25,5,4,0,0)
Treads <- c(0,1,3,4,2,4)


# Genotype likelihoods. Ignore how the genotype likelihoods are calculated here
# genotype likelihood assuming the error is the same for all reads
# NB! For real data we have four alleles and we cannot calculate it like this, because the error rate is different for each read
gCC <- (1-e)^Creads * (e/3)^Treads
gCT <-  ( 0.5*(1-e) + 0.5 * e/3 )^(Treads+Creads)
gTT <- (1-e)^Treads * (e/3)^Creads
GL<-rbind(gCC,gCT,gTT)
colnames(GL) <- paste("ind",1:6)

cat("Genotype likelihoods:\n")
print(GL)

Let's try to calculate the likelihoods assuming that the T allele frequency () is 0.3 or 0.1

In [6]:
## NB: theta is the frequency of the T allele (theta_T). The C allele frequency is 1-theta
calculateLogLike <- function(theta,GL){
   #p(z|θ) under HWE, Z = number of T alleles = CC,CT,TT
   pZ  <- c(pZ_CC= (1-theta)^2 ,pZ_CT= 2*theta*(1-theta), pZ_TT= theta^2 )
   sum( log( colSums(GL*pZ) ))
}

theta <- 0.3
cat("\n log-likelihood with T allele frequency theta_T =",theta,"\n")
calculateLogLike(theta , GL)

theta <- 0.1
cat("\n log-likelihood with T allele frequency theta_T =",theta,"\n")
calculateLogLike(theta , GL)

Lets plot the likelihood surface

In [7]:
thetas <- 1:99/100
ll <- sapply(
  thetas,
  function(x) calculateLogLike(x,GL)
)
plot(thetas,ll,ylab="Log likelihood",xlab="T allele frequency (theta_T)",type="l")

To find the maximum we use a EM algorithm which has two steps

E-step:

M-step:

Therefore in each iteration of the EM algorithm we need to calculate the posterior probability of the genotype given the frequency. For this we use bayes formula which can be simplified because

  • Why can we do that?

In the second part we use the posterior probabilities to get the expected number of C and T alleles.

Since our parameter is the T allele frequency , the M-step is the expected fraction of T alleles

(if you instead wanted the C allele frequency you would swap for in the numerator, which gives ).

  • Explain the 2 and the 12 in the above equations.

Lets run the EM algorithm

In [8]:
## NB: theta is the frequency of the T allele (theta_T). The C allele frequency is 1-theta
EMgeno<-function(theta,GL){ #numeric optimazition EM
  ## Q(Z), for Z = number of T alleles: CC,CT,TT = 0,1,2
  #p(x|z)p(z|θ)
   w0<-GL[1,]*(1-theta)^2
   w1<-GL[2,]*2*theta*(1-theta)
   w2<-GL[3,]*theta^2

  ## p(z|θ,x)
  # p(x|θ)= \sum_z p(x|z)p(z|θ) =
  # p(x|Z=0)p(Z=0|θ)+p(x|Z=1)p(Z=1|θ)+p(x|Z=2)p(Z=2|θ)
   pX <- w0 + w1 + w2
  # p(z|θ,x) = p(x|z) p(z|θ) / p(x|θ)
   p0 <- w0/pX
   p1 <- w1/pX
   p2 <- w2/pX

  ## theta_T^(n+1) = E[# T alleles] / E[# alleles in total]
   thetaNew <- sum( p1+2*p2 ) / sum( 2*p0 + 2*p1 + 2*p2 )
   return(thetaNew)
}


maxIter <- 10
output <- matrix(NA,nrow=maxIter+1,ncol=3)
colnames(output)<- c("iter","theta","LL")
#starting point
theta <- c(0.2)

for(i in 0:maxIter){
  #calculate likelihood and print (not used by the EM)
  output[i+1,] <- c(i,theta,calculateLogLike(theta,GL))
  cat("theta_T=",output[i+1,"theta"],"logLike=",output[i+1,"LL"],"iteration",output[i+1,"iter"],"\n")

  #update theta (the EM steps)
  theta <- EMgeno(theta,GL)
}

3. Coin toss - how to find the maximum likelihood for a binomial¶

Let be the outcome of a series of coin tosses (the data) where each 0 corresponds to the outcome tail and each 1 is the outcome of a head. To estimate the frequency () we can write up the likelihood as

To find the maximum likelihood we can choose to maximize with or without the binomial coefficient

In [11]:
## simulate 10 coin tosses
set.seed(1)     # so the numbers below are the same every time the notebook is run
theta_true <- 0.5
( X <- rbinom(10,1,theta_true) )

k <- sum(X)

cat("Number of heads",k,"\n")
  1. 0
  2. 0
  3. 1
  4. 1
  5. 0
  6. 1
  7. 1
  8. 1
  9. 1
  10. 0
Number of heads 6

To find the maximum we can work on any function that is proportional to the probability of the data which is called the likelihood. We can also choose to work on the log-likelihood. As can be seen below, they have their maximum in the same place.

In [12]:
thetas <- 1:99/100

likBinom <- dbinom(k,10,thetas)
plot(thetas,likBinom,ylab="Binom likelihood",xlab="Frequency (theta)",type="l",main="Likelihood - Binom(k=sum X,p=theta,n=N) ")
abline(v=k/10,col="red");legend("topright","Maximum\n likelihood",lty=1,col="red")

likProd <- sapply(thetas, function(x) prod(c(1-x,x)[X+1]) )
plot(thetas,likProd,ylab="prod likelihood",xlab="Frequency (theta)",type="l",main="Likelihood - without binomial coefficient")
abline(v=k/10,col="red");legend("topright","Maximum\n likelihood",lty=1,col="red")

plot(thetas,log(likBinom),ylab="Binom log-likelihood",xlab="Frequency (theta)",type="l",main="log-Likelihood - Binom(k=sum X,p=theta,n=N) ")
abline(v=k/10,col="red");legend("topright","Maximum\n likelihood",lty=1,col="red")
